evidence.pashto: Our first sentences describe things, not actions. English says “The door is open”. Pashto says دروازه خلاصه ده. The noun comes first, then the description, then the present form of “is”. Use دی with masculine singular nouns, ده with feminine singular nouns, and دي with plural nouns such as اوبه (water). You do not need a separate word for English “it” here. On Day 2 we will learn actions and the S–O–V rule.

evidence.pashto: Muhammad Jan: “Yesterday you said زه اوبه څښم — I drink water. Today, when speaking to a familiar friend, say ته اوبه څښې — you drink water. The ending changes from ـم to ـې. We can join two complete clauses: ته کوټه پاکوې او زه پر څوکۍ کښېنم — You clean the room, and I sit on the chair. Each clause has its own subject and verb. Use informal ته with peers; when addressing respected elders, a different polite form will be taught tomorrow.”

evidence.pashto: Saleha points to the water: “Yesterday you learned هغه اوبه څښي — he/she drinks water. Now say زه اوبه څښم — I drink water.” Compare څښي (he/she drinks) with څښم (I drink). Many present-tense first-person verbs end in ـم. Verb endings communicate who is doing the action, so Pashto can sometimes omit the pronoun when context is clear. The verb still usually comes after the object. Some verbs change their stems too: learn the complete form, not just an ending.

evidence.pashto: Ms Hameed: “You have learned ته کتاب لولې — you read a book (speaking to one familiar friend). When addressing an elder, a teacher, an unfamiliar adult or several people, use تاسې کتاب لولئ. The polite/plural verb generally ends in ـئ instead of the informal ـې. The same تاسې form can refer to one respected person or a group. Look at the listener and the context. In some speech you will also hear تاسو; we use تاسې for consistency in these lessons.”

evidence.pashto: Muhammad Jan: “Yesterday you said زه اوبه څښم — I drink water. Today, when speaking to a familiar friend, say ته اوبه څښې — you drink water. The ending changes from ـم to ـې. We can join two complete clauses: ته کوټه پاکوې او زه پر څوکۍ کښېنم — You clean the room, and I sit on the chair. Each clause has its own subject and verb. Use informal ته with peers; when addressing respected elders, a different polite form will be taught tomorrow.”
evidence.englishContext: Authored inline text; reviewer must distinguish examples, alternatives and UI labels.

evidence.pashto: Saleha points to the water: “Yesterday you learned هغه اوبه څښي — he/she drinks water. Now say زه اوبه څښم — I drink water.” Compare څښي (he/she drinks) with څښم (I drink). Many present-tense first-person verbs end in ـم. Verb endings communicate who is doing the action, so Pashto can sometimes omit the pronoun when context is clear. The verb still usually comes after the object. Some verbs change their stems too: learn the complete form, not just an ending.
